screens.title: Introduction to Shader Graph for Visual Effects
screens.narratorSegment: Shaders control how every pixel looks on screen. In this lesson you'll learn what a shader is, why Shader Graph makes shader creation accessible, and how to build simple, efficient unlit effects for visual flair. We'll focus on practical, hands-on patterns: using input nodes like Time and Position, combining math and color nodes to animate a property, and connecting those results to the Master Node so your material renders in the scene. You'll also learn the essential compatibility requirement: Shader Graph works with URP or HDRP. A concrete example we'll build step-by-step is a pulsing glow that blends between two colors using a sine wave driven by the Time node. I'll show a common pitfall — forgetting to switch the render pipeline — and explain why performance matters because every shader runs on the G P U per pixel. By the end you'll be able to create an Unlit Shader Graph, expose properties to the Material Inspector, and test the effect on a simple sphere or plane. Think about one object in your current project that could use a shader-driven glow — how would that change its presence in the scene?

screens.title: What is a Shader?
screens.narratorSegment: A shader is a small program that runs on the G P U to decide how each pixel of a 3D surface appears. Practically, it defines color, transparency, and how a surface reacts to light. This is different from a C P U script because shaders run massively in parallel across many pixels and frames, so they must be concise and performant. A concrete example: a lit material shader computes a base color, applies lighting calculations like metallic and smoothness, and outputs the final shaded pixel. For many visual effects, though, an Unlit shader is preferable because it avoids lighting math and gives artists full control over color and emission. A common misconception is that shaders are only for complex realism; in fact they are the same mechanism that creates stylized, cartoon, or UI-like effects. Another misconception is that shaders require hand-written G P U code; Shader Graph democratizes creation by letting you connect nodes instead of writing HLSL. Takeaway: understand a shader as a per-pixel program, choose Unlit when you want consistent color and emissive effects, and always keep efficiency in mind since GPUs execute shader operations for every pixel rendered. What pixel-level behavior in your scene would you control with a shader?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › What is a Shader?
Definition

Shader — the per-pixel program

Shaders run on the GPU and compute each pixel's final color and transparency. They are compact, parallel programs used for both realistic materials and stylized effects.

Unlit Shader
No lighting
Lit Shader
Includes lighting parameters
Concrete example

A simple lit shader uses Base Color, Normal, Metallic and Smoothness inputs to compute shaded pixels, while an Unlit shader simply outputs a color or texture that ignores scene lights.

Common misconception

People often think shaders must be hand-coded. Shader Graph lets you construct shader logic with nodes, making shader design accessible to artists while still compiling to GPU-friendly code.

Why performance matters
  • Shaders run per pixel each frame. Extra math or texture samples increase GPU cost.
  • Prefer simple node networks for mobile or dense scenes to keep frame rates stable.
Key Takeaway

Think of shaders as the final word on a pixel's appearance. Choose Unlit for stylized emission and keep calculations minimal.

screens.title: Shader Graph Editor & Master Node
screens.narratorSegment: Shader Graph provides a visual canvas where node outputs flow into a final Master Node that defines the material's properties. The Master Node acts as the shader's contract with the render pipeline: its inputs determine what the engine will expect for each pixel. For an Unlit Master you typically feed Color and Alpha. For a Lit Master you feed Base Color, Normal, Metallic, Smoothness, Emission and more. A concrete workflow: create a Shader Graph asset, open it, place input nodes like Color or Texture 2D Asset, transform data with math nodes, and connect the final result to the Master Node. A common misunderstanding is that any node visible in the graph will affect rendering; in truth, only nodes whose outputs are connected through to the Master Node change the shader. Another important point: Master Node type must match your intent. Using a Lit Master when you want a simple emissive effect can introduce unwanted lighting calculations. Key practice: keep the network readable by grouping related logic, naming exposed properties clearly, and saving frequently so changes apply to the Material Inspector. What Master Node inputs will you expose next time you author a material?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › Shader Graph Editor
Editor anatomy

Canvas, nodes, and the Master Node

Assemble input, math, color and utility nodes on the canvas and feed their result to the Master Node, which defines the final shader outputs used by the render pipeline.

Example connection

Connect Color → Multiply (intensity) → Master Color. Without the final connection, the Multiply node produces no visible effect in the scene.

Master Node types
Unlit Master
Color, Alpha, Alpha Clip
Lit Master
Base Color, Normal, Metallic, Smoothness, Emission
Misconception check

If you choose a Lit Master but don't provide normals or metallic inputs, the engine will still calculate lighting using defaults. This can change your expected appearance.

Key Takeaway

Match Master Node type to your visual goal and ensure final outputs are connected to see changes in the scene.

screens.title: Input Nodes: Time, Position, UV, Texture
screens.narratorSegment: Input nodes supply the raw data your shader manipulates. Time is essential for animation: it provides continuously changing values you can feed into Sine or Multiply to create loops. Position provides per-vertex or per-pixel coordinates which you can use for world-space effects like pulsing based on object height. UV gives texture coordinates useful for scrolling or sampling textures. Texture 2D Asset lets you sample image data to drive color, patterns, or masks. A concrete example: to scroll a texture you connect Time into a Tiling And Offset node's Offset input and feed the modified UV into a Texture 2D Asset sampler; the texture will visibly move across the surface. A common misconception is that Time always yields a normalized range; instead, Time outputs a growing value and you often combine it with Multiply and Sine to create usable ranges. Another pitfall is mixing spaces — Position in object space vs world space changes how a gradient aligns. Takeaway: pick the input node that matches the data you need, transform it carefully with math nodes, and always check space conventions when using Position or UV coordinates. Which input node will you experiment with first?

Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › Input Nodes

Input Nodes

Time, Position, UV and Texture samplers provide the fundamental data your shader transforms into visible effects.

Time
Drive animations
Position
Spatial effects
UV
Texture coordinates
Texture 2D Asset
Sample images
Concrete example

Make a scrolling texture by sending Time into Tiling And Offset, then use the changed UV to sample a Texture 2D Asset. The texture will appear to shift across the model.

Space conventions & pitfalls
  • Position in object space moves with the object; in world space it’s fixed to the scene.
  • Time increases continuously; combine it with Multiply or Sine to control amplitude and frequency.
Key Takeaway

Choose the right input node to provide the data you need, and pay attention to coordinate spaces when using Position or UV.

screens.title: Math Nodes: Sine, Lerp, Multiply, Remap
screens.narratorSegment: Math nodes are the workhorses of Shader Graph. Sine creates smooth oscillations, Multiply scales a value, Lerp blends between two inputs based on a t factor, and Remap converts one range into another. Together they let you turn a raw Time value into a usable intensity for color blending. A concrete construction: Time → Multiply (speed) → Sine → Remap to convert the Sine's -1..1 range into 0..1, then feed that into Lerp between two Color properties. A common misconception is that Lerp performs easing — it linearly blends; if you want smoothing you'll need additional math such as Smoothstep. Another pitfall is forgetting to clamp values where needed; Remap can include clamping to prevent overshoot. When using math nodes, be mindful of data types: Vector1 vs Vector3, and ensure the nodes you connect accept compatible types. Takeaway: learn to combine a small set of math nodes to shape behavior precisely, then expose control properties like speed or amplitude so designers can fine tune without editing the graph. Which blend parameter will you expose as a material property? Math Nodes: Sine, Lerp, Multiply, Remap means use sine for oscillation, multiply for scale, remap to convert ranges, and lerp to blend between values; expose controls for speed and amplitude.. In practical terms, use math nodes to transform inputs into usable animation and blends. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › Math Nodes

Math Nodes

Transform inputs into the shapes and ranges you need for blending and animation.

Sine
Oscillates between -1 and 1
Multiply
Scales values
Remap
Convert ranges
Lerp
Linear blend between A and B by T
Concrete example

Create a pulsing intensity: Time × speed → Sine → Remap (-1..1 to 0..1) → use as T in Lerp between two colors or multiply a color by intensity.

Type compatibility

Ensure you connect Vector1 outputs to float inputs and Vector3/4 to vector inputs. Some nodes accept multiple types but others are strict.

Common Mistake

Expecting Lerp to ease results. Lerp is linear; add Smoothstep or custom curves for eased blends.

Key Takeaway

Combine a few math nodes to convert Time into usable blend factors and expose speed for designer control.

screens.title: Build a Color-Transition Unlit Shader — Step by Step
screens.narratorSegment: Let's build a simple unlit shader that blends between two colors over time. Start by creating an Unlit Shader Graph asset in a URP or HDRP project and open the editor. Add a Color property named _ColorA and another named _ColorB. Next add a Time node; this provides the running time value. Multiply Time by a Vector1 property called _Speed to control how fast the blend cycles. Feed the product into a Sine node to create an oscillation. The Sine node outputs values between -1 and 1; add a Remap node to convert that range to 0–1 so it can be used as a blend factor. Add a Lerp node and connect _ColorA to A, _ColorB to B, and the Remap output to T. Finally, connect Lerp output to the Color input of the Unlit Master Node and save the graph. Create a Material using the shader, assign it to a sphere, and run the scene. A common mistake is forgetting to save the Shader Graph — changes won't appear in the scene until you save. Also confirm your project is using URP or HDRP, as Shader Graph assets require one of those pipelines. Which color pair will you try first?

keyIdea.text: Create an Unlit graph, add Color and speed properties, convert Time with Sine and Remap, Lerp between colors, and connect to the Master Node.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › Color-Transition Shader
Quick steps
1. Create Unlit Graph
2. Add Color props
3. Time × Speed → Sine
4. Remap -1..1 → 0..1
5. Lerp → Master Color
Explanation
  • Time provides a continuously increasing value used as the animation driver.
  • Sine produces a smooth oscillation which we remap to a 0–1 range for blending.
  • Lerp blends between two color properties using the remapped oscillation as the blend factor.
Example material properties
_ColorA: neon blue (HDR), _ColorB: hot pink, _Speed: 2.0
Concrete test

Create a sphere named PulsingSphere, assign the Material that uses the graph, and run the scene. Tweak _Speed to make the transition faster or slower.

Common Mistake

Not saving the graph or not using URP/HDRP will make the material appear black or unchanged.

Key Takeaway

A small chain of nodes transforms Time into a designer-friendly blend between colors; expose speed and color for easy tuning.

screens.title: PulsingGlow Shader — Detailed Build and Material Setup
screens.narratorSegment: This guided build expands the pulsing example into a production-ready PulsingGlow shader. First, ensure URP is active. Create an Unlit Shader Graph named PulsingGlowShader and add a Color property _GlowColor set to HDR so it can emit brightness. Add a Vector1 property _PulseSpeed default 2.0. Add the Time node, multiply Time by _PulseSpeed, and feed that into Sine to produce an oscillation. Use Remap to change -1..1 to a 0.5..1.5 range so the glow never fully dims. Multiply _GlowColor by this intensity output to combine color and pulse. Connect the product to the Color input of the Unlit Master Node and save. Create a Material called PulsingGlowMat and assign the shader. Apply the Material to a sphere or plane and run the scene. Adjust _GlowColor and _PulseSpeed in the Material Inspector at runtime to see immediate changes. A common mistake is forgetting to set HDR on the Color property when you want strong emission. Another is setting alpha to zero by accident. Takeaway: expose the right properties and test them in the Material Inspector for fast iteration. Which property will you expose next for artist control?

keyIdea.text: Expose _GlowColor and _PulseSpeed, drive Sine-based intensity, multiply to combine color and intensity, save and assign a Material for live tweaking.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › PulsingGlow Shader
Node network summary
_GlowColor (Color HDR) × (Remapped Sine(Time × _PulseSpeed)) → Color on Unlit Master. _PulseSpeed is a Vector1 property exposed to the Material Inspector.
Material setup
  1. Create Material PulsingGlowMat.
  2. Select Shader Graphs/PulsingGlowShader as its shader.
  3. Assign to a 3D object and adjust properties at runtime.
Example defaults

_GlowColor: neon blue HDR, _PulseSpeed: 2.0, Remap Out range: 0.5–1.5 to avoid full darkness.

Common mistakes & checks
  • Forgot to set project to URP/HDRP — shader may render black.
  • Not saving the graph after edits — scene won't update.
  • Alpha unintentionally set to 0 — object appears invisible.
Key Takeaway

Expose the color and speed you want artists to tweak. Test in the Material Inspector for fast iteration.

screens.title: Hands-on: PulsingGlow Practical Steps and Testing
screens.narratorSegment: This activity walks you through the practical steps to create, apply and iterate on the PulsingGlow effect. Start in a URP project and create a 3D Sphere named PulsingSphere. Create an Unlit Shader Graph called PulsingGlowShader and add two properties: _GlowColor (Color, HDR) and _PulseSpeed (Vector1, default 2). In the graph add Time, Multiply, Sine and Remap nodes to produce a pulse value, then Multiply that pulse by _GlowColor and connect to the Unlit Master's Color. Save the graph, create the Material PulsingGlowMat, choose your shader, and assign the material to the sphere. Run the scene. While running, tweak _GlowColor and _PulseSpeed in the Material Inspector to observe immediate changes. A useful test is to set _PulseSpeed to 0.1 and 4.0 to compare slow and fast pulses. screens.title: Unlit vs Lit Shaders
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between Unlit and Lit shaders is a key design decision. Unlit shaders bypass scene lighting and simply output color and alpha, making them ideal for stylized, emissive, or UI-like effects that should remain consistent regardless of scene lights. For example, a health-bar overlay or holographic UI plane typically uses Unlit. Lit shaders, on the other hand, incorporate normals, metallic, smoothness and other inputs to react to scene lighting, producing realistic material responses. If you need reflections, shadows, or interaction with dynamic lights, choose a Lit shader. A common misconception is that Unlit is cheaper in every case; while Unlit avoids lighting math, complex Unlit networks with many texture samples or heavy math can still be expensive. Another pitfall is using Lit when you want full control of color — lit materials will be influenced by the environment, possibly washing out your intended hue. Takeaway: pick Unlit for consistent emissive visuals and Lit for physically-plausible materials that must respond to scene lighting. screens.title: Common Mistakes and Performance Considerations
screens.narratorSegment: There are a few recurring mistakes and performance concerns when creating shaders with Shader Graph. First, pipeline mismatch: Shader Graph requires URP or HDRP; using the built-in render pipeline will often produce black or missing materials. Second, disconnected nodes: a node with no path to the Master Node has no effect, which is easy to forget in larger graphs. Third, wrong Master Node type: choosing Lit when you need Unlit can introduce unexpected lighting. Performance is the other major area: shaders run per pixel and each texture sample, expensive math operation, or branching increases G P U cost. For example, sampling the same texture multiple times is more expensive than sampling once and reusing the result. Also avoid unnecessary high-frequency trigonometry on every pixel when a cheaper approximation will do. Always test on target hardware and profile shader cost. A useful workflow is to start simple, verify visuals, then incrementally add detail while watching performance. Takeaway: ensure compatibility, keep node networks connected and simple, and profile early. Which performance test will you run first on your shader? fullNarratorScript:
Shaders control how every pixel looks on screen. In this lesson you'll learn what a shader is, why Shader Graph makes shader creation accessible, and how to build simple, efficient unlit effects for visual flair. We'll focus on practical, hands-on patterns: using input nodes like Time and Position, combining math and color nodes to animate a property, and connecting those results to the Master Node so your material renders in the scene. You'll also learn the essential compatibility requirement: Shader Graph works with URP or HDRP. A concrete example we'll build step-by-step is a pulsing glow that blends between two colors using a sine wave driven by the Time node. I'll show a common pitfall — forgetting to switch the render pipeline — and explain why performance matters because every shader runs on the G P U per pixel. By the end you'll be able to create an Unlit Shader Graph, expose properties to the Material Inspector, and test the effect on a simple sphere or plane. Think about one object in your current project that could use a shader-driven glow — how would that change its presence in the scene?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain what a shader does, use Unity's Shader Graph editor to create an Unlit shader, animate shader properties using Time and math nodes, and choose appropriate nodes for color, texture sampling, and utility tasks. Each objective is actionable: you will define a shader's role in rendering and point to where shader logic lives on the G P U, then open Shader Graph and assemble a working node network that produces a visible effect. You'll also expose properties so designers can tweak colors and speeds via the Material Inspector. A concrete example is building a pulsing color shader: you will add a Time node, transform the output with Sine and Remap, and Lerp between two color properties. Finally, you'll know common failure modes such as using the wrong render pipeline or leaving nodes disconnected, and you'll be ready to profile shader cost. These skills matter because shaders are efficient per-pixel programs that, when authored carefully, produce high-quality effects while preserving runtime performance. Which objective feels most relevant to your next project?

These objectives translate directly into tasks you'll perform in a project. You'll set up URP or HDRP so Shader Graph assets render correctly. You'll create an Unlit Shader Graph, expose a color property so a designer can tint an effect, and add a Vector1 property to control pulse speed. A concrete practice is making a pulsing sphere: expose _GlowColor and _PulseSpeed, connect Time through Sine and Remap to drive Lerp or Multiply, and save the graph to see the result in a Material. You'll also practice debugging: check that nodes are connected, confirm the Master Node type matches your intention, and ensure you saved the graph before expecting changes in the scene. Finally, you'll learn to keep shaders performant by minimizing texture samples and expensive math. These are the skills that move a visual effect from prototype to a production-ready material, and they reduce iteration friction between artists and programmers. Which practical task will you try first in your project?

A shader is a small program that runs on the G P U to decide how each pixel of a 3D surface appears. Practically, it defines color, transparency, and how a surface reacts to light. This is different from a C P U script because shaders run massively in parallel across many pixels and frames, so they must be concise and performant. A concrete example: a lit material shader computes a base color, applies lighting calculations like metallic and smoothness, and outputs the final shaded pixel. For many visual effects, though, an Unlit shader is preferable because it avoids lighting math and gives artists full control over color and emission. A common misconception is that shaders are only for complex realism; in fact they are the same mechanism that creates stylized, cartoon, or UI-like effects. Another misconception is that shaders require hand-written G P U code; Shader Graph democratizes creation by letting you connect nodes instead of writing HLSL. Takeaway: understand a shader as a per-pixel program, choose Unlit when you want consistent color and emissive effects, and always keep efficiency in mind since GPUs execute shader operations for every pixel rendered. What pixel-level behavior in your scene would you control with a shader?

Shader Graph provides a visual canvas where node outputs flow into a final Master Node that defines the material's properties. The Master Node acts as the shader's contract with the render pipeline: its inputs determine what the engine will expect for each pixel. For an Unlit Master you typically feed Color and Alpha. For a Lit Master you feed Base Color, Normal, Metallic, Smoothness, Emission and more. A concrete workflow: create a Shader Graph asset, open it, place input nodes like Color or Texture 2D Asset, transform data with math nodes, and connect the final result to the Master Node. A common misunderstanding is that any node visible in the graph will affect rendering; in truth, only nodes whose outputs are connected through to the Master Node change the shader. Another important point: Master Node type must match your intent. Using a Lit Master when you want a simple emissive effect can introduce unwanted lighting calculations. Key practice: keep the network readable by grouping related logic, naming exposed properties clearly, and saving frequently so changes apply to the Material Inspector. What Master Node inputs will you expose next time you author a material?

Input nodes supply the raw data your shader manipulates. Time is essential for animation: it provides continuously changing values you can feed into Sine or Multiply to create loops. Position provides per-vertex or per-pixel coordinates which you can use for world-space effects like pulsing based on object height. UV gives texture coordinates useful for scrolling or sampling textures. Texture 2D Asset lets you sample image data to drive color, patterns, or masks. A concrete example: to scroll a texture you connect Time into a Tiling And Offset node's Offset input and feed the modified UV into a Texture 2D Asset sampler; the texture will visibly move across the surface. A common misconception is that Time always yields a normalized range; instead, Time outputs a growing value and you often combine it with Multiply and Sine to create usable ranges. Another pitfall is mixing spaces — Position in object space vs world space changes how a gradient aligns. Takeaway: pick the input node that matches the data you need, transform it carefully with math nodes, and always check space conventions when using Position or UV coordinates. Which input node will you experiment with first?

Math nodes are the workhorses of Shader Graph. Sine creates smooth oscillations, Multiply scales a value, Lerp blends between two inputs based on a t factor, and Remap converts one range into another. Together they let you turn a raw Time value into a usable intensity for color blending. A concrete construction: Time → Multiply (speed) → Sine → Remap to convert the Sine's -1..1 range into 0..1, then feed that into Lerp between two Color properties. A common misconception is that Lerp performs easing — it linearly blends; if you want smoothing you'll need additional math such as Smoothstep. Another pitfall is forgetting to clamp values where needed; Remap can include clamping to prevent overshoot. When using math nodes, be mindful of data types: Vector1 vs Vector3, and ensure the nodes you connect accept compatible types. Takeaway: learn to combine a small set of math nodes to shape behavior precisely, then expose control properties like speed or amplitude so designers can fine tune without editing the graph. Which blend parameter will you expose as a material property? In practical terms, use math nodes to transform inputs into usable animation and blends. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Multiply Time by a Vector1 property called _Speed to control how fast the blend cycles. Feed the product into a Sine node to create an oscillation. There are a few recurring mistakes and performance concerns when creating shaders with Shader Graph. First, pipeline mismatch: Shader Graph requires URP or HDRP; using the built-in render pipeline will often produce black or missing materials. Second, disconnected nodes: a node with no path to the Master Node has no effect, which is easy to forget in larger graphs. Third, wrong Master Node type: choosing Lit when you need Unlit can introduce unexpected lighting. Performance is the other major area: shaders run per pixel and each texture sample, expensive math operation, or branching increases G P U cost. For example, sampling the same texture multiple times is more expensive than sampling once and reusing the result. Also avoid unnecessary high-frequency trigonometry on every pixel when a cheaper approximation will do. Always test on target hardware and profile shader cost.
